awd_titl_txt: The 2025 Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) Workshop; Newark, New Jersey; March 14-15, 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
This award provides support to the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) Workshop to be held at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) between March 14-15, 2025. The HamSCI Workshop is an annual workshop that aims to bring together members of the amateur radio and professional radio space science communities for mutual benefit. This workshop series has led to cutting-edge work in the fields of space physics, citizen science, and the use of crowd-sourced ionospheric data. The 2025 HamSCI Workshop will feature prominent leaders in radio science, space science, and space weather. The theme of the 2025 workshop is “HamSCI’s Big Year” and refers to the immense level of organization and activity undertaken by HamSCI participants over the past year to support scientific studies of the 14 October 2023 annular and 8 April 2024 total solar eclipses. 

During this two-day workshop, professionals and amateurs come together to give oral and poster presentations, equipment demonstrations, and have informal discussions and networking related to both amateur radio and applicable scientific fields. Several distinguished speakers have been invited. The 2025 workshop will continue building on topics from past HamSCI meetings, including the use of amateur radio techniques for observing and understanding the physics of space weather, including the ionospheric response to solar flares and geomagnetic storms, and space weather effects on radio wave propagation. The workshop will feature prominent leaders in radio science space weather. It will also serve as a development meeting for the HamSCI Personal Space Weather Station (PSWS), a project funded through the NSF Aeronomy Distributed Array of Small Instruments (DASI) program. This conference would enable (a) development of open technologies and observation networks that can be used in conjunction with existing space science and space weather infrastructure, (b) creation of materials, projects, and products that can be used by groups such as schools, museums, and other educational institutions to teach space and radio science, and (c) enhancement of public relations and outreach through venues and organizations such as the American Radio Relay League (ARRL), CQ Magazine, the HamSCI online presence, the American Geophysical Union, and the NSF Coupling, Energetics, and Dynamics of Atmospheric Regions (CEDAR) program.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This grant supported the the 2025/2026 HamSCI (Ham Radio Science CItizen Investigation) Workshop. The major goals of the workshop were to:

1. Enable amateur radio operators and professional scientists to come together to share ideas, techniques, and results pertaining to space weather and space science research questions.

2. Facilitate the development of instrumentation for a new network of HamSCI Personal Space Weather Stations.

3. Identify techniques to use data from existing amateur radio networks in a scientific manner.

4. Use amateur radio techniques for the characterization and study of ionospheric phenomena such as impacts from solar eclipses, traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs), Sporadic E, solar flares, plasma bubbles, auroral substorms, and geomagnetic storms.

5. Develop an enhanced understanding and community awareness of ionospheric effects resulting from forcing due to both space and terrestrial weather.

The major activity of this project was the 2025 HamSCI Workshop. Unfortunately, funding for the 2025 HamSCI Workshop (which was held at the New Jersey Institute of Technology) was not released in time for the 2025 Workshop. Instead, with permission from the NSF, the 2025 workshop funding was used for the 2026 HamSCI workshop, which was held at the Central Connecticut State University (CCSU) March 14 - 15, 2026, and hosted by the Amercaio Radio Relay League (ARRL). The 2026 workshop was a resounding success-over 125 in-person attendees particpated in the workshop over the two days. This number comprises "professional" scientists, citizen scientists, students, and amateur radio enthusiasts. Additionally, there were 150 registered virtual attendess.

The workshop provided several opportunities for training and professional development on several fronts. First, project funds were used to support the participation student, citizen scientist, and early career professionals at the workshop. This allowed them to interact with other workshop attendess and disseminate their own HamSCI results. Second, the workshop featured three tutorials on various topics-each designed to provide a basic understanding of some of the scienticic topics, and analysis and observational techniques used in the field. In addition to the tutorial previously mentioned, the two others were "Introduction to Baseband Processing" and "Meteor Scatter Science". Additionally, the workshop had five tech demonstrations, which provided attendees with a more interactive training experience. 

The workshop's results have been disseminated through several modes of communication:

- By e-mail via the HamSCI Google Group, which has over 1500 members.

- Via the workshop''s website (https://hamsci.org/hamsci2026).

- Via YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLuapIzKwhZN-S6mHhPtTmFiOoTj_dRs_n), which has video recording of all of the workshop's presentations and (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCjiMbEPNl4) which is a recap video of the workshop.  

- The workshop was featured in a lengthy write-up in the August edition of ARRL's QST magazine (see attached PDF). QST has an estimated readership of over 100,000; paying members of ARRL are automatically subscribed to QST.

- Results and advancements discussed at the HamSCI workshop are also regularly communicated to the space science community via posters and oral presntations at workshops and conferences such as NSF's CEDAR Workshop, which was held in June 2026, and the AGU Annual Meeting, which will happen in December 2026.
